title: Foundations of Financial Regulation and Supervision
summary: An eight-module induction for new regulatory staff covering why we regulate, the authority's powers, risk-based supervision and a first supervisory case.
intro: This training programme equips new joiners and developing staff with a clear understanding of why financial services are regulated, how the authority uses its powers and how risk-based supervision works in practice.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give new and developing staff a structured induction into the purpose, powers and working methods of a financial regulatory authority, from authorisation through supervision to enforcement. Participants leave able to place their own role in the wider regulatory lifecycle and to approach a first supervisory case with confidence and sound professional standards.
sections.What It Covers: Why financial services are regulated, the authority's objectives and powers, the regulatory toolkit, risk-based supervision, the lifecycle from authorisation to enforcement, international standards and peer assessment, ethics and independence, and a first supervisory case.
Intended Audience: Graduates, new joiners and staff in their first two years at a financial regulatory authority
Staff moving into supervisory, authorisation, policy or enforcement roles from support or other functions
Secondees and staff from related public bodies needing a grounding in financial supervision
Learning Objectives: Explain the market failures and public interest objectives that justify financial regulation
Describe the authority's mandate, powers and accountability, and how its functions fit together
Apply the principles of risk-based supervision to prioritise firms and issues
Identify the main international standards and how they shape the authority's work
Recognise the ethical standards, independence and conduct expected of a supervisor
Work through a first supervisory case from information gathering to proposed response
sections.Structure and Format: Eight modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a four-day induction programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines short briefings with exercises and a running case study, and modules can be selected or tailored to the authority's structure and mandate.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: No prior regulatory experience is required. A general interest in financial services and the economy is helpful.
Core Reading: IOSCO (2017), Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (2024), Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision
IAIS (2019, as updated), Insurance Core Principles and Common Framework for the Supervision of Internationally Active Insurance Groups
FATF (2012, as updated), International Standards on Combating Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism and Proliferation: The FATF Recommendations
IMF (2010), The Making of Good Supervision: Learning to Say "No" (Staff Position Note SPN/10/08)

modules.title: Why We Regulate Financial Services
modules.summary: The economic and public interest case for financial regulation, the market failures it addresses and the costs and limits of intervention.
objectives: Explain the market failures that justify regulating financial services
Distinguish prudential, conduct, market integrity and financial crime objectives
Recognise the costs, trade-offs and limits of regulation
syllabus: Information asymmetry, externalities, moral hazard and systemic risk
Prudential, conduct and market integrity objectives compared
Lessons from financial crises and regulatory failures
The costs of regulation: proportionality and unintended consequences

modules.title: The Authority: Mandate, Objectives and Powers
modules.summary: How a regulatory authority is constituted, what it is required to achieve, the powers it holds and how it is held to account.
objectives: Describe the authority's statutory objectives and how they are balanced
Identify the main powers available to the authority and their limits
Explain how independence and accountability work together
syllabus: Legal basis, governance and statutory objectives of the authority
Rule-making, authorisation, information-gathering and intervention powers
Independence, transparency and accountability to government and the public
Working with other domestic authorities and the national FIU

modules.title: The Regulatory Toolkit
modules.summary: The range of tools the authority uses to achieve its objectives, from rules and guidance through supervision to intervention, and how to choose between them.
objectives: Distinguish rules, principles, guidance and supervisory expectations
Match supervisory tools to the risk and the desired outcome
Explain when and how the authority escalates its response
syllabus: Rules-based and principles-based regulation
Guidance, consultation and communicating expectations to the industry
Supervisory tools: reviews, visits, thematic work and data returns
Escalation ladder: from feedback letters to formal intervention

modules.title: Risk-Based Supervision in Practice
modules.summary: How the authority assesses the impact and probability of harm, allocates scarce resources and decides where supervisory attention should go.
objectives: Explain impact and probability as the basis of risk-based supervision
Apply a simple risk assessment framework to a firm
Prioritise supervisory work across a portfolio of firms
syllabus: Impact, probability and the authority's risk appetite
Risk assessment frameworks and supervisory ratings
Proactive, reactive and thematic supervision
Proportionality: matching intensity to risk

modules.title: The Regulatory Lifecycle: From Authorisation to Enforcement
modules.summary: How firms and individuals move through the regulatory lifecycle, and how authorisation, supervision, enforcement and resolution teams hand over and work together.
objectives: Describe each stage of the lifecycle and the function responsible for it
Explain how information flows between authorisation, supervision and enforcement
Identify points where risks are most often missed or lost in handover
syllabus: The gateway: authorisation and fit and proper standards
Ongoing supervision and the firm's supervisory relationship
Referral to enforcement and the range of outcomes
Firm failure, orderly exit and resolution

modules.title: International Standards and the Global Regulatory Architecture
modules.summary: The international bodies that set standards for financial regulation, how their standards are applied nationally and how the authority is assessed against them.
objectives: Identify the main international standard-setters and their remits
Explain how international standards are adopted and assessed
Recognise the importance of cross-border cooperation and information exchange
syllabus: The FSB, Basel Committee, IOSCO, IAIS, FATF, CPMI and IOPS
Core principles and how they translate into national frameworks
Peer reviews, mutual evaluations and international assessments
Supervisory colleges, memoranda of understanding and information sharing

modules.title: Ethics, Independence and the Professional Supervisor
modules.summary: The personal standards expected of a supervisor, the threats to independence and objectivity, and the habits that underpin credible supervisory judgement.
objectives: Explain the ethical duties and conduct standards that apply to regulatory staff
Recognise conflicts of interest, capture and other threats to independence
Apply professional scepticism and sound judgement in everyday work
syllabus: Confidentiality, conflicts of interest, gifts and hospitality
Regulatory capture and maintaining independence from industry
Professional scepticism, challenge and willingness to act
Accountability for decisions and recording the rationale

modules.title: Your First Supervisory Case: Integrated Workshop
modules.summary: Brings the programme together in a facilitated case study in which participants assess a firm, form a view of its risks and propose a proportionate supervisory response.
objectives: Gather and interpret information on a firm's business and risks
Form an initial risk assessment and identify key concerns
Propose and justify a proportionate supervisory response
syllabus: Case briefing: the firm, its business and the information available
Identifying red flags and framing supervisory questions
Agreeing a risk view and proposed actions in small groups
Workshop: presenting the case to a mock supervisory panel

related.title: Assessing Board Effectiveness
related.summary: An eight-module programme showing supervisors how to assess how a board really works, from papers and decisions to culture and challenge, culminating in case-study interviews.

related.title: Core Supervisory Skills: Business Models, Governance and Risk Governance Panels
related.summary: A three-day workshop taking supervisors from business model analysis through governance interviews to a risk governance panel, using running case studies and role plays.

related.title: How Financial Firms Work: Business Models and Financial Statements for Supervisors
related.summary: An eight-module programme helping supervisors understand how financial firms make money, read their accounts and identify capital, liquidity and business model risks.

related.title: Supervising Compliance in Practice: Masterclass Series
related.summary: Ten half-day masterclasses showing supervisors how to test whether firms' compliance arrangements work in practice across core compliance areas.

related.title: Supervisory Risk Assessment Toolkit
related.summary: A ten-module toolkit taking supervisors through the full firm risk assessment cycle, from business model and governance analysis to panels, risk ratings and findings.

related.title: Core Professional Skills for Regulatory Staff
related.summary: An eight-module practical programme building the core writing, analysis, meeting, challenge, presentation and data skills that regulatory staff need every day.
